clue.text: Intimidate fellow ranch owner

parts.note: to intimidate is to cow, bully into submission
a fellow is a man, a chap

explanation.surface: A bullying cattle baron throws his weight around on the ranch.
explanation.definitionFit: A cattle farmer or rancher who keeps cows is called by this name, especially in the American West.

clue.text: Officer limped off, having acted in accordance with other's wishes

definitions.text: having acted in accordance with other's wishes

parts.note: CO is the standard abbreviation for Commanding Officer

indicators.note: off here means gone wrong or bad, so the letters of limped are mixed up

explanation.surface: An injured officer hobbled away, obeying someone else's orders.
explanation.definitionFit: To obey or go along with a request is the verb behind this past tense.

clue.text: Man gains weight

parts.note: to gain a prize or victory is to win it, giving wins
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: Someone is putting on the pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is not a person in general but a man's name, as in Churchill's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A male first name, famously Churchill's, so a fellow by that name is an example of a man.

clue.text: States for the most part I'm going round the bend for a radioactive element

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, its final letter being dropped

parts.note: the States is America, the USA

indicators.note: the letters of I'm go around the bend, enclosing it

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
a U-bend, so U stands for the bend

explanation.surface: A traveller in America mostly loses his mind over a radioactive substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going round the bend' poses as the idiom for going mad, but the bend is a U-bend, as in plumbing, and 'going round' is a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Element 95, a synthetic radioactive metal named after the Americas, used in smoke detectors.

clue.text: Stray from Bolton?

explanation.surface: A wanderer from a northern English town.
explanation.walkthrough: Bolton Wanderers is a football club in Bolton, a town near Manchester; one of its players or fans could be called by its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A stray is a roaming, homeless creature, a drifter; and the Bolton football team are called Wanderers, so a player from Bolton is one.

clue.text: Man student

parts.note: read as someone who studies mankind, humans and their societies, rather than a male student

explanation.surface: A male pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: This scientist studies the human race, its cultures and its development, so is a student of man.

clue.text: Appreciate something on hand

explanation.surface: Value whatever you have available.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is two words run together: 'dig it' is slang for enjoy or appreciate. 'On hand' looks like 'available' but means literally on your hand.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig something is slang for liking it; and a finger is a part attached to the hand.

clue.text: Backward movement by way out monarch first

indicators.note: first places the monarch's letter at the front of the other piece

parts.note: R stands for rex or regina, king or queen
an egress is an exit, a way out

explanation.surface: A king is leading a retreat out of the palace.
explanation.definitionFit: To go back to an earlier, less developed state; as a noun, a going back.

clue.text: Go round or up to the gallery

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word or is read from bottom to top

parts.note: the Tate is the famous London art gallery

explanation.surface: Take turns, or go up to the gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: To spin or turn on an axis, like a wheel.

clue.text: Ordinary alternative for the use of land

definitions.text: alternative for the use of land

explanation.surface: Plain choices about how to use your plot.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the phrase literally: a piece of land may be used as a common (open public land) or as a garden.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday phrase means unremarkable, everyday; and taken literally it offers two choices of land use, public field or private plot.

clue.text: Pea gives skin disease to all in France

parts.note: mange is a skin disease of animals caused by mites
tout is French for all, and the to is absorbed into it

explanation.surface: A vegetable passes on a rash to everyone in France.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is French for 'eat all', a variety of pea eaten pod and all.
explanation.definitionFit: A variety of flat edible pod, a type of garden pea eaten whole, also called snow pea.

clue.text: US soldier obtained a leg of lamb

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier
obtained means got

explanation.surface: An American serviceman picked up some meat for dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: A French cookery term for a mutton or lamb joint cut from the hind limb.

clue.text: Silvery metal ignited by one with an unpleasant smell going round

parts.note: ignited means lit

indicators.note: the smell goes around the one, enclosing it

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A shiny metal set alight gives off a nasty pong.
explanation.definitionFit: The lightest metallic element, soft and silver-white, used in batteries.

clue.text: Negotiate afresh but lose ground

explanation.surface: Talk again about terms but end up giving way.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense splits the word as RE-TREAT, to treat (negotiate) again.
explanation.definitionFit: To treat again is to deal or bargain once more; to withdraw is to fall back, as an army does.

clue.text: Nine, you say, suffer boredom

indicators.note: suffer is read as be damaged, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: the letter U sounds like the word you

explanation.surface: A speaker says you'll suffer tedium nine times over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suffer' signals the anagram of NINE plus U.
explanation.definitionFit: A French loan word for weariness and listlessness, a world-weary tedium.

clue.text: One from a mountainous country asleep twitchily in the corner

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go in between the two letters of the corner

parts.note: NE, the north-east corner, as on a map

indicators.note: twitching is restless movement, so the letters of asleep are jumbled

explanation.surface: A Himalayan visitor dozes fitfully in the corner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twitchily' turns ASLEEP into EPALES, which goes 'in' NE.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Himalayan kingdom home to Everest is described by this word.

clue.text: Strange dog lent me a deposit

indicators.note: strange means odd or unusual, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A peculiar dog was loaned to me as a security.
explanation.definitionFit: A deposit or accumulation, something lodged, such as silt settling.

clue.text: Injurious arrest?

parts.note: an unjust detention, the kind for which a person might sue the police, hinted by the question mark

explanation.surface: A harmful detention by the police.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means unjust or unlawful, and an unlawful detention is a common legal phrase.

clue.text: Healing ointment said to be used at the castle

parts.note: balm is a soothing ointment
oral means spoken, said aloud

explanation.surface: A soothing ointment spoken of for use at a royal castle.
explanation.walkthrough: BALMORAL is the British royal family's castle in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish residence of the British royals on Deeside is this castle.

clue.text: One to leave a quintet inside with spirit from Scandinavia

parts.note: one is the indefinite article a

indicators.note: the quintet's letters go inside the word for leave

parts.note: to leave is to quit
a quintet is five, the Roman numeral V

explanation.surface: Someone departing a band of five takes a drink of schnapps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is A, not I. 'inside' puts AV (a, quintet) into QUIT, giving QUAVIT after the opening A.
explanation.definitionFit: A caraway-flavoured Scandinavian schnapps, the name meaning water of life.

clue.text: Do not encourage dunderhead to vandalise tree

parts.note: the head of dunder, its first letter

indicators.note: vandalising damages the tree, so its letters are wrecked into a new order

explanation.surface: A fool is warned off from wrecking a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dunderhead' looks like 'idiot' but is read as the head (first letter) of 'dunder'; 'to vandalise' makes ETER from TREE.
explanation.definitionFit: To discourage or put off someone from acting, by fear or doubt.

clue.text: Teaching you in France with one on the inclusion of sex-appeal

indicators.note: the inclusion of means the sex-appeal word is included within the other letters

parts.note: tu is French for you
one is the Roman numeral I
taken as written
IT is an old term for sex-appeal

explanation.surface: A French tutor is giving lessons with an alluring quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' meaning sex-appeal comes from the 1920s film star Clara Bow, the It girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Instruction or coaching, as given by a tutor.

clue.text: Drunk into a small container

explanation.surface: Someone tipsy is stuffed into a tin.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition: food that has been canned is put into a can.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for intoxicated; and also preserved in a tin, sealed in a metal pot.

clue.text: Tanks of water and air, strangely enough

parts.note: aqua is Latin for water

indicators.note: strangely signals that the letters of air are oddly reordered

explanation.surface: Tanks hold water and air, oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tanks of water' wants to be the definition; the water is AQUA and only 'Tanks' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Glass tanks for keeping fish, the Latin plural of a fish tank's name.

clue.text: Blue flush

explanation.surface: A face going blue and then red.
explanation.walkthrough: Each definition is the first word of a phrase: royal blue is a deep blue, and a royal flush is the top poker hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal blue is a bright deep shade; a royal flush is ace to ten in one suit in poker.

clue.text: Madly caring about sweetheart nationality

indicators.note: madly signals the letters are crazily rearranged

parts.note: the heart of sweet is its middle letter E

explanation.surface: A lover cares wildly about the nationality of their darling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is a link; 'sweetheart' is not a lover but the heart (middle letter) of 'sweet'.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to Greece, an adjective for Greek origin or style.

clue.text: Labourer number five in force

indicators.note: in places the numeral inside the word for the force

parts.note: the navy is a fighting force
the Roman numeral for five is V

explanation.surface: A workman is the fifth man in the armed services.
explanation.walkthrough: A NAVVY is a British word for a manual labourer on roads or railways, from 'navigator', the canal diggers.
explanation.definitionFit: A British term for a manual worker on building or digging projects.

clue.text: Doubt about faith in the infernal world!

parts.note: Dis is the classical underworld, the realm of the dead
faith means belief

explanation.surface: Questioning religion in hell!
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' and 'in' are link words; Dis is the Roman god of the underworld and, in Dante, the city of hell.
explanation.definitionFit: Doubt and incredulity, the refusal to accept something as true.

clue.text: Entailed adjustment at the meridian

indicators.note: an adjustment changes the order of the letters of entailed

explanation.surface: A change was required at the meridian.
explanation.walkthrough: The International Date Line roughly follows the 180th meridian.
explanation.definitionFit: The line roughly along 180 degrees longitude where the calendar day changes.

clue.text: In being offbeat on a lute not in any particular key

indicators.note: in being means the answer exists inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A lutenist plays offbeat music without a fixed key.
explanation.definitionFit: Music without a tonal centre, as in Schoenberg, avoids any home key.
